subject: Fluid Mechanics
summary: viscosity, surface tension and compressibility, hydrostatic pressure and manometry, forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces, buoyancy and metacentric height, and liquids in rigid-body rotation

questions.text: A block weighing 150 N with a 0.4 m × 0.4 m base slides down a plane inclined at 20° on an oil film 1 mm thick, as shown. Its steady (terminal) speed is 0.5 m/s. Assuming a linear velocity profile in the film, the dynamic viscosity of the oil (in Pa·s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: At terminal speed the weight component along the plane equals the viscous drag: W sin θ = τA = μ(V/h)A.
Exam tip: 1 Pa·s = 10 poise, so this oil has μ = 6.4 P.

questions.text: A clean glass tube of 2 mm internal diameter is dipped vertically in water (σ = 0.073 N/m, contact angle 0°). The capillary rise (in mm, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Capillary rise h = 4σ cos θ/(ρ g d), from balancing surface tension round the perimeter against the weight of the raised column.
Exam tip: Mercury (θ ≈ 130°) gives a negative h: capillary depression. Halving the diameter doubles the rise.

questions.text: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of diameter d (surface tension σ) over the outside pressure is
solution: Concept: A soap film has two surfaces (inside and outside). Force balance on half the bubble: Δp × πd²/4 = 2 × σπd.
Δp = 8σ/d
Exam tip: Liquid droplet (one surface): 4σ/d; liquid jet (cylinder): 2σ/d.

questions.text: The bulk modulus of water is 2.2 GPa. The increase in pressure needed to reduce a given volume of water by 0.5 % (in MPa) is ______
solution: Concept: K = −Δp/(ΔV/V).
Exam tip: This is about 1100 m of water head for only 0.5 % volume change, which is why liquids are treated as incompressible.

questions.text: Pipes A and B carry water and are connected by a differential U-tube mercury manometer, as shown. The centre of A is 300 mm above the centre of B and the mercury level in the limb on B's side stands 150 mm higher than in the limb on A's side. The pressure difference p<sub>A</sub> − p<sub>B</sub> (in kPa, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Start at A, add ρgh going down, subtract going up, and end at B.
Take the lower mercury surface as datum and let B be y above it, so A is (y + 0.3) above it.
p<sub>A</sub> + ρ<sub>w</sub>g(y + 0.3) − ρ<sub>Hg</sub>g(0.15) − ρ<sub>w</sub>g(y − 0.15) = p<sub>B</sub>
Exam tip: The unknown y always cancels; if it does not, a sign is wrong.

questions.text: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high holds water on one side; its top edge is 1.5 m below the free surface, as shown. The depth of the centre of pressure below the free surface (in m, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: F = ρgAh̄ and hcp = h̄ + IG/(A h̄) for a vertical plane.
Exam tip: The deeper the gate, the closer the centre of pressure moves to the centroid.

questions.text: A circular plate of 1.2 m diameter is immersed in water with its plane inclined at 60° to the horizontal and its centre 2 m below the free surface. The vertical depth of its centre of pressure below the free surface (in m, round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: For an inclined plane: hcp = h̄ + IG sin²θ/(A h̄).
IG/A for a circle = d²/16 = 1.44/16 = 0.09 m²
Exam tip: The total force does not depend on the inclination; only the position of the centre of pressure does.

questions.text: The quarter-circle gate AB shown (radius 2 m, width 3 m perpendicular to the paper) holds water above it, with its centre O at the free surface. The magnitude of the resultant hydrostatic force on the gate (in kN, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Horizontal component = force on the vertical projection; vertical component = weight of the water above the curved surface up to the free surface.
FV = ρg b πR²/4 = 9810 × 3 × π = 92.46 kN (downward)
F = √(58.86² + 92.46²) = 109.6 kN, at 57.5° to the horizontal, passing through O
Exam tip: On a circular surface every pressure force is normal to it, so the resultant always passes through the centre.

questions.text: For a plane surface submerged vertically (or inclined) in a liquid, the centre of pressure lies below the centroid because
opts: the area of the plate is large
solution: Concept: The pressure distribution is triangular/trapezoidal, so the larger pressures on the lower part move the line of action of the resultant below the centroid by IG sin²θ/(A h̄).
For a horizontal plane the pressure is uniform and the two points coincide.
Exam tip: The gap IG/(A h̄) → 0 as the plate goes deeper.

questions.text: A rectangular wooden pontoon 1 m long, 0.5 m wide and 0.4 m high (specific gravity 0.7) floats in water with its 0.4 m side vertical. Its metacentric height for rolling about the longitudinal axis (in mm, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: GM = BM − BG with BM = I/V (I = second moment of the waterline plane about the roll axis).
Depth of immersion d = 0.7 × 0.4 = 0.28 m; KB = 0.14 m, KG = 0.20 m
Exam tip: Rolling uses the smaller dimension b; pitching about the transverse axis would use L³ and be far more stable.

questions.text: Which statement about the stability of bodies in a liquid is correct?
opts: A floating body is stable if its metacentre lies above its centre of gravity
A submerged body is stable if its centre of gravity lies above its centre of buoyancy
A floating body is stable only if its centre of gravity lies below its centre of buoyancy
A floating body is stable if its metacentre lies below its centre of gravity
questions.ans: (A) A floating body is stable if its metacentre lies above its centre of gravity
solution: Concept: For a floating body the shift of B on tilting creates a restoring couple if M lies above G (GM > 0).
For a fully submerged body B does not shift, so it is stable only if B is above G.
Exam tip: A floating body can be stable even with G above B (ships), thanks to the metacentre.

questions.text: An open tank contains a 2 m layer of oil (specific gravity 0.85) floating on 3 m of water. The gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank (in kPa, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Pressures of stacked layers add: p = Σρgh.
Exam tip: Express every layer as an equivalent water head first: 0.85 × 2 = 1.7 m of water.

questions.text: An open cylindrical tank of 0.4 m diameter, partly filled with water, is rotated about its vertical axis at 150 rpm. With no water spilling, the difference between the water levels at the wall and at the centre (in m, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Forced vortex (rigid-body rotation): the free surface is a paraboloid with z = ω²r²/(2g).
Exam tip: The volume of a paraboloid is half that of its circumscribing cylinder, so the level rises Δz/2 at the wall and falls Δz/2 at the centre.

questions.text: A stone weighs 50 N in air, 30 N when fully immersed in water and 34 N when fully immersed in an oil. The specific gravity of the oil is
solution: Concept: Loss of weight = buoyancy = ρliquid g V.
In water: 50 − 30 = 20 N; in oil: 50 − 34 = 16 N
Soil = 16/20 = 0.8 (and Sstone = 50/20 = 2.5)
Exam tip: This is the principle of the hydrometer and of finding the density of an irregular solid.

questions.text: A fluid whose apparent viscosity decreases as the rate of shear increases (for example, blood or paint) is called
solution: Concept: Power-law fluid τ = K(du/dy)n: n < 1 pseudoplastic (shear-thinning), n > 1 dilatant (shear-thickening), n = 1 Newtonian.
A Bingham plastic (toothpaste) needs a yield stress before it flows.
Exam tip: Thixotropic fluids thin with the time of shearing, not just its rate.
